Purtenance
PUR-te-nance
noun
A worn-down form of appurtenance, from Old French apartenance (that which pertains or belongs to a thing), Latin appertinere (to pertain, belong to): here the inner parts “belonging” to the carcase—the pluck, the heart, liver, and entrails. It renders the Hebrew qereb, the inward parts.

Biblical Definition

The purtenance is the inward parts of a beast—the pluck, the heart, liver, and entrails that pertain or belong to the body—and the word stands but once in the KJV, in the law of the passover: the lamb is to be roast with fire, his head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof (Exo 12:9). Nothing of the lamb was to be sodden in water nor eaten raw, but the whole—head, legs, and inwards together—was to pass through the fire and be eaten in the night of redemption. The command is emphatic and total: the lamb was to be taken entire, its inward parts not discarded but roasted with the rest, that the household might feed upon the whole sacrifice with nothing left over till the morning (Exo 12:8, 10). The purtenance thus guards a great gospel figure. Christ is our passover, sacrificed for us (1Co 5:7); and as the passover lamb was given whole to the fire and whole to the eating, so the whole Christ is given for His people and received by them—not a Saviour parcelled out, not His hard sayings left on the plate, not His lordship divided from His mercy. The fire that consumed the offering (Lev 1:9) is the figure of the wrath He bore entire; the eating is the faith that feeds on the whole Christ. Nothing of the Lamb is to be left uneaten: head, legs, and purtenance, the whole of Him is our food and our salvation.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PURTENANCE as the pluck of an animal; the inwards or intestines; a corruption of appurtenance.

expand to see more

PURTENANCE, n. — The pluck of an animal; the inwards or intestines; the heart, liver, and entrails. His head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof (Exo 12:9).

PURTENANCE, n. — That which pertains or belongs to the carcase; the inner parts appurtenant to the body of the beast.

PURTENANCE, n. — A worn form of APPURTENANCE, retaining the sense of things belonging to a whole.

APPURTENANCE, n. — That which belongs or pertains to something else; an adjunct or appendage; the parent word.

PURTENANCE — Now obsolete except in the language of Scripture and old husbandry.

Key Scripture

Exo 12:9 — "Eat not of it raw, nor sodden at all with water, but roast with fire; his head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof."

Exo 12:8 — "And they shall eat the flesh in that night, roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs they shall eat it."

Lev 1:9 — "But his inwards and his legs shall he wash in water: and the priest shall burn all on the altar, to be a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD."

1Co 5:7 — "Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us:"

Modern Corruption

A KJV hapax of the passover, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the wholeness of the sacrifice—the whole Lamb given to the fire and to the eating, figuring the whole Christ received entire by faith.

expand to see more

The word rebukes the modern appetite for a parcelled Christ—a Saviour taken in pieces, His comforts kept and His commands declined, His mercy relished and His lordship left on the plate. The passover would have none of it: head, legs, and purtenance, the whole lamb went to the fire and the whole lamb was eaten, and nothing was to remain till the morning. The age loves to choose among the inward parts of the faith, to keep the palatable and discard the purtenance—the hard sayings, the cost, the cross. But a lamb divided is no passover, and a Christ divided is no Saviour. The command that nothing of the Lamb be left uneaten is a standing rebuke to every selective, self-flattering religion that would feed on the Redeemer’s benefits while refusing His yoke.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wholeness of Christ given and received. As the passover lamb was roast entire and eaten entire, so the whole Christ—Prophet, Priest, and King; His atoning death and His righteous rule; His sweet promises and His searching demands—is offered to sinners and is to be received by faith without reserve. Christ our passover is sacrificed for us; let us keep the feast, not with the old leaven of a divided allegiance, but feeding on the whole Lamb. Nothing of Him is to be left over; head, legs, and purtenance, He is wholly ours, and we are to be wholly His.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French apartenance / Latin appertinere (to pertain, belong) — the inward parts belonging to the carcase; the KJV hapax at Exo 12:9, rendering Hebrew qereb, the inwards.

expand to see more

Latin appertinere — to pertain, belong to (from ad- + pertinere); the source of the sense of parts belonging to a whole.

Old French apartenance — that which pertains or belongs; worn down in English to purtenance.

Hebrew qereb (H7130) — the inward part, midst, entrails (Exo 12:9, the purtenance of the passover lamb; Lev 3:3).

Hebrew peder / kāved — the fat and the liver among the inwards, the choicest parts given to the fire (Lev 3:4).

English appurtenance, pertain — the surviving kin, keeping the sense of what belongs or is annexed to a thing.

Usage

"His head with his legs, and with the purtenance thereof—the whole passover lamb, inward parts and all, was to pass through the fire and be eaten in the night of redemption."

"As the lamb was given whole to the fire and whole to the eating, so the whole Christ is given and received—not a Saviour parcelled out, His hard sayings left on the plate."

"Nothing of the Lamb was to be left uneaten; the command rebukes every selective religion that feeds on the Redeemer’s benefits while refusing His yoke."
